what_its_for: Mycophenolate mofetil is a medicine that weakens your immune system on purpose. It is used to prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ (such as a kidney, heart, or liver). It may also be used to treat certain autoimmune conditions where your immune system is attacking your own body, such as lupus nephritis.
how_to_take: Take this medicine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the capsules or tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. You may take it with or without food, but taking it with food can help reduce stomach upset. If you are using the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use and use the measuring device provided. Wash your hands before and after handling this medicine. Avoid breathing in the powder from broken capsules or letting the liquid touch your skin or eyes.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 1,000 mg (1 gram) taken twice a day, about 12 hours apart. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on your condition, weight, and how well your body tolerates the medicine. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — as long as it is not too close to the time of your next dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store capsules and tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep the liquid (oral suspension) in the refrigerator or at room temperature as directed on the label — do not freeze it. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely, following your pharmacist's or local guidelines.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who have infections, colds, the flu, or chickenpox, as this medicine weakens your immune system and makes it harder for your body to fight germs. Do not get live vaccines (such as live flu spray, shingles vaccine Zostavax, or yellow fever vaccine) while taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors, since this medicine increases your risk of skin cancer. Do not take antacids containing magnesium or aluminum at the same time as this medicine — space them apart by at least 2 hours. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should avoid handling broken tablets or capsules.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: signs of serious infection such as high fever, chills, severe sore throat, or wounds that won't heal; unusual bruising or bleeding; blood in your urine or stools; severe stomach pain, vomiting, or diarrhea; signs of a new skin growth, mole, or unusual skin change; confusion, weakness on one side of the body, or changes in vision or speech (these could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you think you may be pregnant.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working to suppress your immune system within a few days of starting it, but its full protective effect in preventing organ rejection builds up over time. You may not notice any change in how you feel, since the medicine works quietly in the background. It is very important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you feel well. Stopping it suddenly can lead to organ rejection or disease flare-ups.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT take this medicine if you are pregnant. It can cause serious birth defects or pregnancy loss. Women who can become pregnant must use two reliable forms of birth control starting 4 weeks before treatment, during treatment, and for 6 weeks after stopping. Men should also use effective contraception during treatment and for 90 days after stopping. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine, as it may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Older adults: Older patients may have a higher risk of certain side effects, including infections. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have severe kidney or liver disease. Children: Dosing in children is based on body size and the transplant type — follow your doctor's specific instructions carefully.
